stem: Approximately what percentage of epileptic patients will have normal EEG between attacks?
explanation: When an EEG is performed in the outpatient setting, it detects epileptiform abnormalities in only 29- 55% of patients in any type of focal epilepsy.
reference: Boutros NN, Galderisi S, Pogarell O, Riggio S. Standard electroencephalography in clinical psychiatry: A practical handbook. 2011. pp. 86-87.

stem: Flattened trace of EEG is a feature seen in
explanation: A significant reduction in voltage with a predominant absence of alpha rhythms, sometimes leading to flat traces, is seen in Huntington disease.

stem: REM sleep includes which of the following physiological features?
options: Increased recall of dreams if awoken
correctAnswer: Increased recall of dreams if awoken
explanation: Because most people awakened during a REM episode recall that they were dreaming, physicians equate REM sleep with dreaming. Dreams that occur during REM sleep possess emotional or intellectual complexity, at least on a superficial level, and rich visual imagery that people readily recall. During REM sleep, in contrast to the accompanying flaccid muscle paralysis, autonomic nervous system activity increases and produces an increased pulse rate, elevated blood pressure, raised intracranial pressure, increased cerebral blood flow, greater muscle metabolism, and, in boys as well as men, erections.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 th Edition. 2023. p. 379.

stem: A patient is administered 1g of dexamethasone at 11PM, and his plasma samples are collected to measure hormone levels on the following morning. Which of the following is correct concerning the physiological changes overnight?
explanation: The dexamethasone suppression test (DST) is used to demonstrate a failure of feedback suppression of ACTH/CRH and continuous production of endogenous cortisol despite administration of exogenous steroid (dexamethasone). Normally administering dexamethasone must reduce cortisol in plasma. This is because of intact HPA function leading to reduced ACTH and CRH. In depression and other psychiatric hypercortisolemic states (also in organic hypercortisolemic states such as Cushing's), this does not occur.

stem: The resting membrane potential of a neuron is around
explanation: A neural membrane at resting potential is about -70mV (meaning that the intracellular side of the membrane is -70mV with respect to the extracellular environment). This resting potential is caused by differences in the relative concentration and permeability of various inorganic ions, particularly sodium, potassium, and chloride, as well as by the active contributions of a sodium-potassium pump.
reference: Carter M, Essner R, Goldstein N, Iyer M. Guide to Research Techniques in Neuroscience, 3 rd Edition. 2022. p. 86.

stem: Which of the following is associated with low levels of cortisol?
explanation: Although increased cortisol levels are typically associated with chronic stress, PTSD is often linked with lower cortisol levels. Further, lower cortisol levels shortly after trauma predict subsequent PTSD severity. This paradoxical finding has been interpreted in term of cortisol binding to the glucocorticoid receptors in a negative feedback loop that promotes homeostasis of the stress response. This proposal posits that lower cortisol in PTSD may result in elevated ongoing activity of the hypothalamic- pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, resulting in exaggerated catecholamine response and subsequent over- consolidation of trauma memories.
reference: Bryant RA. Post‐traumatic stress disorder: a state‐of‐the‐art review of evidence and challenges. World Psychiatry. 2019 Oct;18(3):259-69.

stem: EEG changes in Angelman Syndrome are notable by the age of
explanation: Angelman Syndrome (AS) is characterised by severe developmental delays including marked speech impairment, movement abnormalities, (ataxia, tremor), and unique behaviours such as frequent laughter. Intractable epileptic seizures since early childhood with characteristic EEG abnormalities are present in 80-90% of patients with AS. The onset of epilepsy is most prevalent between 1 and 3 years of age.
reference: Samanta D. Epilepsy in Angelman syndrome: A scoping review. Brain and Development. 2020 Sep 4;1-13.

stem: Which of the following physiological changes are noted after ECT in clinically depressed individuals?
explanation:
Virtually every neurotransmitter system is affected by ECT, but a series of ECT sessions results in the

downregulation of post-synaptic beta-adrenergic receptors, the same receptor change observed with virtually all antidepressant treatments. The effects of ECT on serotonergic neurons remain controversial.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 731.

stem: Regular 3 Hz complexes are seen in EEG of patients with which of the following conditions?
explanation: In patients with absence seizures (petit mal), the EEG produces a characteristic pattern of three-per- second spike-and-wave activity.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 250.

stem: Which one of the following statements is true about normal EEG?
options: The normal dominant alpha rhythm is usually achieved by 8-10 years old.
Closing the eyes usually abolishes the dominant alpha rhythm.
Ongoing delta activity when awake is almost always abnormal in the awake adult.
Beta activity is almost always abnormal in the adult.
The dominant alpha rhythm is seen in the fronto-temporal region.
correctAnswer: Ongoing delta activity when awake is almost always abnormal in the awake adult.
explanation: By mid-adolescence, the EEG essentially has the appearance of an adult tracing. Alpha waves (frequency range 8-13 Hz) are highly rhythmic and constitute the dominant brain wave frequency of the normal eyes-closed awake EEG. Beta waves (frequencies that are faster than the upper 13 Hz limit of the alpha rhythm) are not uncommon in average adult waking EEG studies. Delta waves (frequency of 3.5 Hz or less) are not present in the normal waking EEG, but a prominent feature of deeper stages of sleep. Presence of significant generalised or focal delta waves in the awake EEG is strongly indicative of a pathophysiological process.
reference:
Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp . 998-

999.

stem: Which of the following sleep EEG changes is seen when taking benzodiazepines for insomnia?
explanation: Multiple sleep-related changes including a decrease in sleep latency, increased sleep time, reduced stage 1 sleep, increased stage 2 sleep, reduced REM and Slow Wave Sleep, and REM rebound on cessation are seen with benzodiazepines.

stem: An EEG showing high amplitude repetitive bilaterally synchronous symmetrical polyphasic sharp wave and slow wave complexes, which occur every 4-15 seconds are characteristic of
explanation: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare, predominantly childhood-onset neurologic illness that probably results from a latent or mutant measles (rubella) virus infection of neurons. Alternatively, the body’s aberrant response to this infection causes the illness. Clinicians can confirm a diagnosis of SSPE by finding an elevated measles titre in the CSF. An EEG is also diagnostically helpful: it shows periodic sharp-wave complexes or a burst-suppression pattern. Generalised periodic discharges appear as regular, sharp waves or spikes. They can have a clinical correlate in myoclonic jerks. The EEG pattern of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) also shows periodic discharges. Unlike conventional CJD which typically appears at age 50-64 years, variant CJD (vCJD) typically affects teens and young adults, and the EEG lacks periodic complexes.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 th Edition. 2023. pp. 131-132, 154, 210.

stem: Which of the following brain regions when stimulated via magnetic pulse reduces depression?
explanation:
When using repetitive transcranial stimulation (rTMS) for the treatment of depression, placement of the coil is on the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Research suggests that rTMS results in changes in regional brain activity and metabolism, and that applying rTMS at the left DLPFC can enhance this region’s connectivity with other regions that are crucial for regulating emotional processing. Hardy S et al. Transcranial magnetic stimulation in clinical practice. BJPsych Advances. 2016

Nov;22(6):373-9.

stem: Which stages of sleep are considered as slow wave sleep?
explanation: REM sleep: The eyes undergo rapid movements, and there is a high level of brain activity. Non-REM sleep: There is reduced neuronal activity. Stage 3 and 4 of NREM are grouped as slow wave sleep because the slow delta waves predominate in these two stages.

stem: Which type of EEG trace is expected when eyes are closed during relaxation?
explanation: Alpha waves (frequency range 8-13 Hz) are highly rhythmic and constitute the dominant brain wave frequency of the normal eyes-closed awake EEG.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 998.

stem: 1-2 Hz shaped wave pattern is seen in
explanation: The classic EEG finding in CJD is generalized 1-2 Hz bi- or triphasic sharp- and slow-wave complexes. These may not appear until very late in the clinical course, if at all, and may require repeated testing. The earliest EEG finding is more often rhythmic generalized slowing.

stem: At resting membrane potential which ion is greatest in concentration inside the cell?
explanation: At resting membrane potential, there are more potassium ions inside and more sodium ions outside the plasma membrane. A sodium-potassium pump continually pumps sodium ions out of the cell and potassium ions into the cell.
reference: Carter M, Essner R, Goldstein N, Iyer M. Guide to Research Techniques in Neuroscience, 3 rd Edition. 2022. p. 87.

stem: Orexin (hypocretin) neurons are dysfunctional in which of the following disorders?
explanation:
Narcolepsy is characterised by excessive daytime sleepiness, the intrusion of sleep during periods of wakefulness, and abnormal REM sleep, including sleep-onset REM periods. Cataplexy, or loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions, may also be present. A clear neuropathological substrate has been

identified for narcolepsy with cataplexy: profound loss of orexin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. Orexin neurons are involved in stabilising wakefulness through stimulating release of wake-promoting neurotransmitters (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine, acetylcholine, and histamine). Orexin also stabilises motor movements, allowing normal movement in the day when orexin levels are high and facilitating inhibition of motor movements at night, especially during REM sleep, when orexin level are low. When orexin levels are low in the daytime due to loss of orexin neurons, this destabilises motor movements during the daytime, allowing intrusions of motor inhibition and loss of muscle tone, known as cataplexy, during periods of wakefulness.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5 th Edition. 2021. p. 435.

stem: A 3 month-old newborn undergoes awake EEG investigation to detect seizure activity, but no abnormalities are found. Which of the following waveforms will be prominent in the recording?
explanation: With maturation, EEG activity gradually goes from a preponderance of irregular medium- to high- voltage delta activity (3.5Hz or less) in the tracing of the infant, to greater frequency and more rhythmic pattern. Rhythmic activity in the upper theta-lower alpha range (7 to 8 Hz) can be seen in posterior areas by early childhood, and, by mid-adolescence, the EEG essentially has the appearance of an adult tracing.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 999.

stem: Which of the following associated with neuroendocrine changes during sleep is correct?
options: Cortisol shoots up in slow wave sleep
Prolactin decreases in early morning sleep
explanation: Melatonin regulates circadian rhythms. It has both synchronizing and phase-shifting properties in the regulation of biological rhythms. It reduces during REM sleep.

stem: Which of the following is a posterior pituitary hormone?
explanation: The vasopressor effects of posterior pituitary extracts were first described in 1895. Oxytocin (OT) and vasopressin (AVP) mRNAs are among the most abundant messages in the hypothalamus, being heavily concentrated in the magnocellular neurons of the paraventricular nucleus and the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus, which send axonal projections to the neurohypophysis. These neurons produce OT and AVP (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which is released into the bloodstream, where these peptides act like hormones on peripheral targets.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 969.

stem: Which of the following disorders is characterised by a predominant presence of triphasic waves in EEG?
explanation: Triphasic waves typically consist of generalised synchronous waves occurring in brief runs. They are 1.5-3.0 per second high-voltage slow waves, with each slow wave initiated by a blunt or rounded spike-like transient. Approximately one half of patients with triphasic waves have hepatic encephalopathy. The remainder have other toxic-metabolic encephalopathies.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. pp. 999- 1000.

stem: Mrs. X is a patient with bipolar affective disorder with secondary amenorrhea. The investigation to be done is
explanation: The most common cause of secondary amenorrhoea is pregnancy. Also, anticonvulsants used in bipolar disorder can reduce the efficacy of oral contraceptives.

stem: K complexes during sleep EEG are seen during
explanation: The large multicomponent K-complex and the rhythmic spindle are the hallmarks of NREM stage 2 sleep.
reference: Ioannides AA, Liu L, Kostopoulos GK. The Emergence of Spindles and K-complexes and the role of the dorsal caudal part of the anterior cingulate as the generator of K-complexes. Frontiers in neuroscience. 2019 Aug 7;13:814.

stem: The brain region that acts as monitor of circadian rhythm is
explanation: The key neurobiological regulator of the circadian sleep system is the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus.
reference: Smith PC, Mong JA. Neuroendocrine control of sleep. Neuroendocrine Regulation of Behavior. 2019:353-78.

stem: The levels of ACTH and CRF are increased and play an important role in the neuroendocrinology of
explanation: The normal stress response involves activation of the hypothalamus and a resultant increase in corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF), which in turn stimulates the release of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) from the pituitary. ACTH causes glucocorticoid release from the adrenal gland. In situation of chronic stress, hyperactivity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis leads to excessive glucocorticoid release. Elevated HPA activity is one of the clearest links between depression and the biology of chronic stress. Hypercortisolaemia in depression suggests one or more of the following central disturbances: decreased inhibitory serotonin tone; increased drive from norepinephrine, acetylcholine (Ach), or corticotropin-releasing hormone (CHR); or decreased feedback inhibition from the hippocampus.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5 th Edition. 2021. pp. 270-271. Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 395.

stem: Regarding the neuronal resting membrane potential, which of the following is true?
options: Hyperpolarise with moving out of chloride.
Depolarise with rapid moving out of sodium.
Repolarise with moving out of potassium.
Repolarise with rapid cellular entry of sodium.
Depolarise with rapid cellular entry of potassium.
correctAnswer: Repolarise with moving out of potassium.
explanation: An action potential, also referred to as a spike, is an all-or-none, rapid, transient depolarisation of the neuron’s membrane. An action potential occurs when localised potentials within the neuron sum to bring the membrane voltage to its threshold potential, around -55mV. This triggers the opening of voltage-gated sodium channels, and the rapid influx of sodium ions brings the membrane potential to a positive value. The membrane potential is restored to its normal resting value by the delayed opening of voltage-gated potassium channels and by the closing of the sodium channels. A refractory period follows an action potential, corresponding to the period when the voltage-gated sodium channels are inactivated.
reference: Carter M, Essner R, Goldstein N, Iyer M. Guide to Research Techniques in Neuroscience, 3 rd Edition. 2022. p. 88.

stem: There is a nocturnal surge in the level of growth hormones during which of the following stages of sleep?
explanation: Growth hormone is elevated in the earlier portions of a sleep bout - particularly in slow-wave sleep - and decreases in later sleep phases.
reference: Smith PC, Mong JA. Neuroendocrine control of sleep. Neuroendocrine Regulation of Behavior. 2019:353-78.

stem: Which of the following statement concerning REM sleep is INCORRECT?
options: EEG shows activity similar to awake state
Cardiac activity is similar to awake state
Muscle tone is similar to awake state
correctAnswer: Muscle tone is similar to awake state
explanation:
REM sleep is characterised by faster activity on an EEG – similar to that seen during periods of

wakefulness – as well as distinct eye movements, and peripheral muscle paralysis and loss of muscle tone called atonia. During REM sleep, autonomic nervous system activity increases and produces an increased pulse rate, elevated blood pressure, raised intracranial pressure, increased cerebral blood flow, greater muscle metabolism, and, in boys as well as men, erections.
reference: Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5 th Edition. 2021. p. 413. Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 th Edition. 2023. p. 379.

stem: Which of the following stages of sleep predominates in a neonate?
explanation: Neonates sleep 16-20 hours a day, with about 50% of that time spent in REM sleep.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 th Edition. 2023. p. 383.

stem: Which of the following is an innovative treatment with some beneficial effect in dystonia?
explanation: Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) or transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) may modulate abnormal sensorimotor networks and restore motor control in dystonia.
reference: Lizarraga KJ et al. Update on current and emerging therapies for dystonia. Neurodegenerative Disease Management. 2019 Jun;9(3):135-47.

stem: Infants have a dominant rhythm of which of the following EEG wave frequencies?
explanation: With maturation, EEG activity gradually goes from a preponderance of irregular medium- to high- voltage delta activity (3.5Hz or less) in the tracing of the infant, to greater frequency and more rhythmic pattern. Rhythmic activity in the upper theta-lower alpha range (7 to 8 Hz) can be seen in posterior areas by early childhood, and, by mid-adolescence, the EEG essentially has the appearance of an adult tracing.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 999.

stem: Generalised spike-wave discharges with decreased waves on photic stimulation are seen in EEG of patients with;
explanation: Certain maneuvers can provoke EEG abnormalities in patients suspected of having epilepsy. Hyperventilation and photic stimulation by looking at a stroboscopic light, the two most commonly used techniques, may trigger diagnostic epileptiform discharges and even seizures in patients with a primary or genetic generalised epilepsy.
reference: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 th Edition. 2023. p. 208.

stem: REM rebound on cessation is seen with the use of which of the following?
explanation: Stimulants reduce the total sleep time by decreasing both REM sleep and Slow Wave Sleep. On cessation of stimulants (except modafinil), REM rebound occurs.

stem: The duration of normal sleep latency in healthy adults is
explanation: Sleep latency is measured as the time to sleep onset. It is normally about 15-20 minutes. Sleep latency >30min can be indicative of insomnia.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 439. Stahl SM. Stahl’s Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and Practical Applications, 5 th Edition. 2021. p. 421.

stem: Which one of the following classes of drugs increases beta activity on EEG?
explanation: Benzodiazepines generate a significant amount of diffuse beta activity. Both benzodiazepines and barbiturates typically produce excessive beta (fast) activity, which may be a telltale sign of surreptitious drug use.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 999. Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman’s Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 th Edition. 2023. p. 210.

stem: Which one of the following is characteristic of REM sleep?
options: Reduced recall of dreaming if awoken
Upward ocular deviation with few or no movements
explanation: Because most people awakened during a REM episode recall that they were dreaming, physicians equate REM sleep with dreaming. Dreams that occur during REM sleep possess emotional or intellectual complexity, at least on a superficial level, and rich visual imagery that people readily recall. REM sleep is characterised by faster activity on an EEG – similar to that seen during periods of wakefulness – as well as distinct eye movements, and peripheral muscle paralysis and loss of muscle tone called atonia. stem: A 42-year-old man is a journalist. He goes to sleep at 10PM every night and wakes up at 530AM every morning. If he volunteers for a sleep study using a polysomnogram, the time from sleep onset to the first REM episode will be
explanation: A typical night’s sleep has four or five cycles of sequential stages, each lasting 90-110 min. The end of the first sleep cycle is marked by a brief period of arousal before the onset of REM sleep (at approximately 90 min). As the night progresses, the amount of time spent in delta sleep decreases, with consequent increase in REM sleep. Hence, the first REM period may last 5-10 min, while the last, just before waking, may last up to 40 min.
reference:
Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p.

437.

stem: Peak cortisol levels in normal individuals are noted around
explanation: A diurnal variation in ACTH and cortisol levels occurs in humans, with peak cortisol levels occurring around 6:00-7:00 AM.

stem: A 34-year-old patient who is taking sulpiride undergoes EEG investigation for detecting drug-related EEG changes. What would you expect to see?
explanation: Slowing of beta activity with an increase in alpha, theta and delta activity is seen with antipsychotics.

stem: A 47-year-old woman presents with low mood and lethargy. She is noted to have a history of untreated hypothyroidism. Which of the following is inconsistent with a diagnosis of hypothyroidism?
explanation: The most common symptoms of hypothyroidism in adults are fatigue, lethargy, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, change in voice, and dry skin. Signs may also include sexual dysfunction and bradycardia. Primary hypothyroidism is defined by TSH concentrations above the reference range.
reference: Chaker L et al. Hypothyroidism. Lancet. 2017 Sep 23;390(10101):1550-1562.

stem: Regarding major depression, which of the following statements on neuroendocrine abnormalities is correct?
options: Large dose of cortisol exacerbates depressive symptoms
50% of patients show raised cortisol levels
Low levels of corticotrophin releasing factor is found in CSF of patients
Atrophy of adrenal cortex is seen in 20% of patients
correctAnswer: 50% of patients show raised cortisol levels
explanation: Many depressed patients have a high level of cortisol in plasma and urine. It is now known that 50% of depressed patients exhibit hypercortisolemia.

stem: Mr. Y presents to the emergency department with a history of apathy and weight loss. On further investigations, he has hyponatraemia and hyperkalemia. What is his possible diagnosis?
explanation: Addison’s disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) is characterised by chronic glucocorticoid and/or mineralocorticoid deficiency due to failure of the adrenal cortex. It should be suspected in all acutely or chronically ill patients with general fatigue or severe weakness and unexplained dehydration, hypotension, weight loss, fever, abdominal pain and hyperpigmentation. Key lab characteristics include hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and (especially in children) hypoglycemia. Psychiatric symptoms include apathy, anhedonia, fatigue, and depressed mood.
reference: Barthel A et al. An update on Addison’s disease. Experimental and Clinical Endocrinology & Diabetes. 2019 Feb;127(02/03):165-75.

stem: Peak cortisol level in normal physiological states is seen at
explanation: A diurnal variation in ACTH and cortisol levels occurs in humans, with peak cortisol levels occurring around 6:00-7:00 AM.

stem: Which one of the following is not a characteristic feature of Kleine-Levin syndrome?
explanation: Kleine-Levin syndrome is a rare syndrome of ‘periodic somnolence and morbid hunger’, occurring almost exclusively in male adolescents. It is characterised by periods lasting from days to weeks of attacks of hypersomnia, accompanied by excessive food intake.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 452.

stem: Which of the following receptor on stimulation leads to sleep onset?
explanation: The noradrenergic rapid eye movement (REM)-OFF neurons in locus coeruleus and cholinergic REM- ON neurons in tegmentum show a reciprocal firing pattern. The REM-ON neurons fire during REM sleep whereas REM-OFF neurons stop firing during REM sleep. http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17704548
